newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland teeters on brink after IRA bombing.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland teeters on brink after IRA bombing.

text.p: Northern Ireland appeared to be on the brink of renewed sectarian warfare on Wednesday after the IRA admitted bombing Britain's army base in the province and risked retaliation by its Protestant Loyalist enemies.
British Prime Minister John Major led a chorus of calls to Loyalist guerrillas not to avenge the IRA attack on the Lisburn army base but to abide by a two-year ceasefire.
"The Provisional IRA are trying to provoke a general return to violence in Northern Ireland. We must not let them succeed. I appeal to all Loyalists not to fall into this trap," Major said.

The Loyalists' umbrella organisation, the Combined Loyalist Military Command, made no statement after a meeting on Tuesday, raising tensions among the 40 percent Catholic minority and 60 percent Protestant majority alike.
Spokesmen for political parties close to the Loyalists also called on them to stand by the truce which has allowed the organisations a seat at the Belfast peace talks.
"We should avoid as best we can the cycle of violence that undoubtedly would take us to hell and back again," David Ervine of the Progressive Unionist Party (PUP) told Reuters.

For 25 years Catholics have been in the front line of vengeful attacks by Loyalists who have killed 900 of them in retaliation for violence by the Irish Republican Army, which is fighting to end British rule of the province.

The IRA statement, admitting its guerrillas carried out the bombing of Britain's army headquarters in Lisburn, south of Belfast, appeared to signal the start of a new campaign in Northern Ireland itself after a two-year respite.
The attack humiliated British security, wounded 20 soldiers and 11 civilians, and was the most audacious IRA strike since the guerrillas fired mortars into Heathrow airport in 1994.
Since ending its own 17-month ceasefire in February, the IRA has struck targets in British cities and a British army base in Germany but has avoided attacking Northern Ireland itself.

The tactical switch followed fresh statements by Britain and Ireland that the IRA's political wing would not be allowed to join peace talks under way in Belfast until the IRA renewed its ceasefire and signed up to principles of non-violence.

The talks group pro-British Unionists and the Irish nationalist Social Democratic and Labour party of John Hume but the absence of Sinn Fein means the guerrillas whose war is at the heart of the conflict is not represented.

Major was unbowed by the IRA statement. "Sinn Fein have excluded themselves more clearly than ever," he told reporters, hours after Sinn Fein President Gerry Adams said he was willing to hold talks with the British government at a moment's notice.

There was speculation in political circles that the IRA was gambling that it could force concessions out of Major before he holds elections by May next year which opinion polls show he would lose to a resurgent Labour party.
The governments refuse to invite Sinn Fein until the IRA declares a truce but the IRA has accused them of trying to disarm Republican guerrilla units using the talks as a cover.

"The resolution of the conflict demands an inclusive negotiated settlement. This is not possible unless and until the British Government faces up to its responsibilities," the IRA statement, issued to Irish media, said.
A two-year Anglo-Irish peace plan has courted collapse since its launch because of British insistence that the IRA disarm.
But Britain abruptly changed tack to demanding that the guerrillas renounce violence and disarm in stages after the IRA resumed its war with a bomb at London's docklands in February.
